subject: Private deployment telemetry: export formats, trace-sampling, and SIEM tuning
messages:

Subject: Observability requirements for private Redwood deployment

Hi Ava,

Thanks for taking this on. We're getting close to spinning up the private VPC deployment for Redwood and the security team has a few specific questions around observability export and SIEM integration before we proceed to acceptance testing. High level asks:

- Which export protocols do you support natively in Private deployments (syslog, Splunk HEC, OTLP/OTEL collector, Kafka, S3 archives)?
- For SIEMs (Splunk/QRadar/ArcSight) do you provide structured mapping examples (field names + example events)?
- Trace sampling: how do you surface Redwood span/span attributes, and what hooks exist so we can apply our sampling policy centrally?
- Retention/egress: we need an architecture sketch showing what stays in-customer VPC vs what (if anything) leaves to Redwood control plane.

We're trying to finalize SIEM ingestion on our side next week. Can you send a short checklist and any sample config snippets? Attaching our SIEM intake spec (scc-customer-siem-spec.xlsx).

Appreciate it,
Craig Dalton
Director, Security Engineering
Oregon Bank

--Attachment: scc-customer-siem-spec.xlsx (spreadsheet; columns: timestamp, host, facility, severity, message, redwood_model, request_id)

From: Ava Chen <ava_chen@redwood.ai>

Cc: kimberly_park@redwood.ai, marissa_cole@redwood.ai
Date: Tue, 02 May 2028 10:03:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Observability requirements for private Redwood deployment

Craig — thanks, forwarding to our Private deployment security and observability team. I've attached a concise onprem observability checklist and a sample OTLP config that we typically hand off for customer SIEM testing. High level answers inline:

- Protocols supported: syslog (RFC5424), Splunk HEC, OTLP/OTEL collector (gRPC & HTTP), Kafka (Avro/JSON), S3-compatible object store for batched exports.
- SIEM mapping: we provide field mapping templates for Splunk HEC and a CSV mapping that matches the columns you shared.
- Trace sampling: Redwood exposes an OTLP-compatible trace sink. We surface span attributes: redwood.request_id, redwood.model, redwood.instance_id, redwood.seq_len, redwood.prompt_hash. Sampling hooks let you apply client-side sampling in your OTEL collector or server-side policies via our config layer (we document sampling policy examples).
- Retention/egress: In Private mode nothing is sent to Redwood's hosted tenants by default. Control plane telemetry (health-checks/usage-only) is optional and anonymized; any logs/PII can be configured to remain in-customer VPC and exported to your SIEM.

I'll let Kimberly add the exact Splunk HEC example and Marissa add recommended retention windows for security logs. Proposed next step: 30-minute sync tomorrow to walk through the checklist while you run a test ingestion.

Best,
Ava Chen
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
ava@redwood.ai
--Attachment: onprem-obsv-checklist.pdf (checklist; one-pager)

From: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.ai>
To: Samir Patel <samir.patel@oregonbank.com>, Craig Dalton <craig.dalton@oregonbank.com>
Cc: ava_chen@redwood.ai, marissa_cole@redwood.ai
Date: Thu, 04 May 2028 11:15:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Observability requirements for private Redwood deployment

Samir / Craig — added technical detail below; pasting examples you can drop into your collector/SIEM.

1) Splunk HEC: we support both event-per-request and batched events. For production Private deployments we recommend batching (batch size 500 events or 5MB, whichever comes first) with persistent local spool on the forwarder. Benefits: lower TLS handshake overhead and better throughput.

2) Log structure: Redwood logs are JSON-structured by default when the model is in structured-output mode. For unstructured text generation you get a JSON envelope that includes metadata plus the raw text. Example event (JSON):
{
  "timestamp": "2028-05-04T18:12:34Z",
  "host": "redwood-infer-01",
  "service": "redwood-inference",
  "redwood_model": "gpt-open-13b",
  "request_id": "req_7f3a9b",
  "severity": "info",
  "message": "generation_complete",
  "token_count": 142
}

3) Trace sampling / span attributes: we recommend preserving these attributes on the client collector: redwood.request_id, redwood.model, redwood.instance_id. If you run sampling at the OTEL collector, use a parent-based sampler with a fast-path for requests that match your high-value criteria (e.g., high dollar transactions, admin flows). We also expose a low-overhead trace hook that emits a 1-line minimal-trace for every request (trace_id + request_id + duration) if you want to keep coarse-grained metrics for every call and only sample full traces intermittently.

4) Authentication & transport: Splunk HEC over HTTPS with token auth is standard; for on-prem we recommend MTLS where possible. For syslog we support TLS-wrapped RFC5424. For Kafka ensure topic partitioning aligns with your ingestion throughput and set retention policies per your compliance needs.

5) Retention guidance (recommended):
- Security-critical logs (auth/events): 2y cold + 90d hot
- Application request logs: 90d hot + 1y cold
- Sampled traces (full spans): 90d
- Minimal per-request traces (1-line): 1y

6) Sample config: I've attached a trimmed OTLP collector config and a Splunk HEC mapping CSV. Notable entries: use asynchronous batch exporter, enable attribute drop for PII fields at the collector if needed, and configure backpressure to avoid local queue saturation.

If you'd like, we can spin up a short-lived test forwarder in your VPC and validate a blue-green switch for ingestion during a maintenance window.

Thanks,
Kimberly Park
Security & Trust, Redwood Inference
kimberly_park@redwood.ai
--Attachment: redwood-otlp-sample.yaml (OTEL collector snippet)
